AI.motivation: To reconcile reversible unitary dynamics of quantum many-body systems with the emergence of irreversible macroscopic hydrodynamics, and to understand the role of the observer's temporal resolution in establishing genuine transport coefficients like friction and viscosity.
AI.method: A data-driven framework combining generalized Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (gEDMD) with the Mori-Zwanzig projection, expanding the observable dictionary to include spin currents and extracting Navier-Stokes coefficients from a chaotic XXZ spin chain across varying temporal coarse-graining scales.
AI.result: The mechanical elasticity ($c^2$) is preserved from exact unitary dynamics (reversible). Friction ($γ$) and kinematic viscosity ($ν$) oscillate around zero under exact evolution. Only with finite temporal coarse-graining ($Δt_{\rm cg} > 0$) do positive, strictly dissipative coefficients emerge after a distinct crossover timescale.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic friction in isolated quantum systems is not an intrinsic property but an emergent phenomenon contingent on the observer's temporal resolution; genuine irreversible transport requires finite coarse-graining of unitary dynamics.

title: Dynamical Signatures of Floquet Topology in Wave Packet Dynamics
summary: Periodically driven quantum systems, known as Floquet systems, provide a versatile platform for engineering novel topological phases absent in static settings. However, dynamically characterizing these non-equilibrium topological invariants remains a challenge. Here, we develop a Floquet perturbation theory in the extended Hilbert space to analytically describe the center-of-mass (CoM) dynamics of a wave packet. When applied to the driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, our theory reveals that the CoM exhibits multi-frequency Zitterbewegung oscillations, whose spectral composition and phase are directly tied to the system's Floquet band structure. Crucially, we find that band inversions at topological phase transitions imprint distinct signatures in the CoM dynamics, including the emergence of low-frequency modes and phase shifts of the oscillatory trajectory. These dynamical signatures offer a practical protocol for detecting Floquet topological invariants, which we demonstrate for both high-frequency and strongly driven regimes. Our work establishes CoM dynamics as a simple and experimentally accessible probe for exploring topological phase transitions in Floquet systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a Floquet perturbation theory to analyze wave packet center-of-mass (CoM) dynamics in periodically driven quantum systems, showing that CoM oscillations reveal multi-frequency Zitterbewegung patterns whose spectral features directly encode Floquet topological invariants, offering an experimentally accessible probe for detecting topological phase transitions.
AI.motivation: Dynamically characterizing non-equilibrium topological invariants in Floquet systems remains a challenge, motivating the need for a practical and experimentally accessible probe to detect topological phase transitions in periodically driven quantum systems.
AI.method: The authors develop a Floquet perturbation theory in the extended Hilbert space to analytically describe the center-of-mass dynamics of a wave packet, and apply it to the driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.
AI.result: The CoM exhibits multi-frequency Zitterbewegung oscillations whose spectral composition and phase are directly tied to the Floquet band structure. Band inversions at topological phase transitions produce distinct signatures: emergence of low-frequency modes and phase shifts in the oscillatory trajectory.
AI.conclusion: CoM dynamics serve as a simple and experimentally accessible probe for exploring topological phase transitions in Floquet systems, demonstrated for both high-frequency and strongly driven regimes.

title: Static-Field Tunneling Ionization in Space-Fractional Quantum Mechanics
comment: Accepted in J. Phys. B; 14 pages, 6 figures
summary: Tunneling ionization in static or slowly varying electric fields is a cornerstone of strong-field physics and provides the entry point for semiclassical descriptions of above-threshold ionization and high-harmonic generation. In conventional quantum mechanics, the Perelomov--Popov--Terent'ev (PPT) theory and its Ammosov--Delone--Krainov (ADK) form yield an ionization rate whose defining feature is an exponential dependence governed by an under-barrier (imaginary-time) action. Here we develop an analytical ADK-like tunneling model within \emph{space-fractional} quantum mechanics, where the quadratic kinetic energy is replaced by the Riesz fractional Laplacian of order $1<α\le2$. Working in a static electric field in the length gauge, we derive a closed-form tunneling exponent for a triangular exit barrier. The fractional kinetic operator deforms the conventional $I_p^{3/2}$ scaling to $I_p^{1+1/α}$ and introduces a characteristic $\sin(π/α)$ factor encoding the complex-phase structure associated with nonlocal dispersion. We position this benchmark relative to prior tunneling studies in fractional quantum mechanics (primarily scattering through model barriers and fractal potentials) and provide a validation protocol for testing the exponent in time-dependent simulations of the fractional Schrödinger equation under a constant field. The result establishes a transparent reference for static-field ionization in nonlocal quantum dynamics and a baseline for strong-field approaches extensions.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical ADK-like tunneling ionization model within space-fractional quantum mechanics (Riesz fractional Laplacian of order 1<α≤2), deriving a closed-form tunneling exponent that deforms the conventional I_p^{3/2} scaling to I_p^{1+1/α} with a sin(π/α) factor encoding nonlocal dispersion effects.
AI.motivation: To extend the established ADK/PPT tunneling ionization theory from conventional quantum mechanics to space-fractional quantum mechanics, providing a benchmark for static-field ionization in nonlocal quantum dynamics and a baseline for strong-field approaches.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of an ADK-like tunneling model using the Riesz fractional Laplacian in the length gauge with a static electric field and triangular exit barrier, yielding a closed-form tunneling exponent.
AI.result: The fractional kinetic operator changes the ionization scaling from I_p^{3/2} to I_p^{1+1/α} and introduces a sin(π/α) factor from nonlocal dispersion; the model is positioned relative to prior fractional quantum mechanics tunneling studies.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a transparent reference for static-field ionization in nonlocal quantum dynamics and a validation protocol for time-dependent fractional Schrödinger equation simulations under constant fields.

title: Quantum Kernels for Parity-Structured Classification: A Hybrid Pipeline
summary: Parity (XOR) classification requires detecting discrete, high-order feature interactions that smooth classical kernels cannot efficiently capture. We study how quantum kernel advantage depends on parity complexity, the number of features entering the XOR rule, and find a clear threshold behavior. We pair a ZZ quantum feature map with binary {0, pi} encoding (features median thresholded before circuit input) to expose parity structure. A binary encoding ablation, RBF SVM trained on the identical {0, pi} features, separates encoding from circuit effects: at low complexity (n = 5 features), binary RBF achieves 83.4% +/- 1.7% and the quantum kernel 81.2% +/- 1.9%, showing encoding drives performance there. At high complexity (n = 11 features, 11 qubits, r = 3 ZZ repetitions), all classical methods collapse to near-random (approx. 50%), binary RBF reaches only 54.3% +/- 1.1%, and the quantum ZZ kernel achieves 66.3% +/- 3.2% (mean +/- std, 10 seeds), a +12.0 percentage-point margin over the binary ablation and approx. 7x higher kernel-target alignment (0.094 +/- 0.020 vs. 0.013 +/- 0.001). These results identify parity complexity as a concrete axis along which genuine quantum kernel advantage, not attributable to encoding alone, emerges.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum kernel advantage on parity (XOR) classification by varying parity complexity. It finds that at low complexity (n=5), encoding drives performance; at high complexity (n=11), the quantum ZZ kernel significantly outperforms classical methods including a binary-encoding RBF ablation (66.3% vs 54.3%), demonstrating genuine quantum kernel advantage not attributable to encoding alone.
AI.motivation: To determine whether quantum kernel methods offer a genuine advantage over classical kernels for parity classification, and to identify parity complexity as a concrete axis where such advantage emerges beyond mere data encoding effects.
AI.method: Pair a ZZ quantum feature map with binary {0, π} encoding (features median-thresholded before circuit input) on parity classification tasks. Compare against classical RBF SVM trained on the identical binary features (binary ablation) to isolate encoding effects. Vary parity complexity (number of features n=5 to 11) and measure kernel-target alignment and accuracy.
AI.result: At n=5, binary RBF achieves 83.4%±1.7% and quantum kernel 81.2%±1.9% (encoding dominates). At n=11, classical methods collapse to ~50%, binary RBF reaches 54.3%±1.1%, while quantum ZZ kernel achieves 66.3%±3.2% — a +12.0 percentage-point margin and ~7× higher kernel-target alignment (0.094 vs 0.013).
AI.conclusion: Parity complexity is a concrete axis where genuine quantum kernel advantage emerges, not attributable to encoding alone, with a clear threshold behavior between low and high complexity regimes.

title: Eigenstate-Selective Entangled Two-Photon Absorption in Monolayer WSe$_2$
summary: We show that the Bell-state phase of a polarization-entangled photon pair controls the biexciton eigenstate distribution produced by entangled two-photon absorption (ETPA) in monolayer WSe$_2$. In a frequency-nondegenerate ladder scheme, two independent valley pathways ($K$ and $K'$) share no intermediate state, so the biphoton phase sets the relative amplitude between them. Within the valley-symmetric limit this phase factorizes from the material response, and the resulting selection rule partitions the excitation among biexciton eigenstates according to the Bell-state phase $\varphi$. The symmetric Bell state ($\varphi = 0$) selectively drives bright eigenstates, while the antisymmetric state ($\varphi = π$) drives the exchange-dark eigenstate. No classical polarization source reproduces this $\varphi$-dependent eigenstate distribution. Including valley dephasing and intervalley scattering at 4~K, the phase-scan visibility exceeds $0.97$ for broadband SPDC ($T_e \sim 100$~fs) with high source purity.

AI.tldr: The Bell-state phase of polarization-entangled photon pairs controls biexciton eigenstate distribution in monolayer WSe₂ via entangled two-photon absorption, with phase-dependent selection rules enabling selective driving of bright (φ=0) or exchange-dark (φ=π) biexciton eigenstates, achieving >0.97 visibility at 4K.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the quantum phase of entangled photon pairs can serve as a control knob for biexciton state selection in monolayer WSe₂, going beyond what classical polarization sources can achieve.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of entangled two-photon absorption in monolayer WSe₂ using a frequency-nondegenerate ladder scheme with two independent valley pathways (K and K'), where the biphoton phase sets relative amplitude between valleys. Valley-symmetric limit allows phase factorization from material response, yielding phase-dependent selection rules.
AI.result: Symmetric Bell state (φ=0) drives bright biexciton eigenstates; antisymmetric Bell state (φ=π) drives exchange-dark eigenstate. Phase-scan visibility exceeds 0.97 at 4K with broadband SPDC (~100 fs) and high source purity despite valley dephasing and intervalley scattering.
AI.conclusion: The Bell-state phase of entangled photons provides a non-classical control mechanism for biexciton eigenstate distribution in monolayer WSe₂, enabling selective excitation that is impossible with classical light sources.

title: Electronic and Photonic Integration of Single Quantum Emitters in 2D Materials
summary: Single-photon sources that are bright, pure, and interference-ready are essential for quantum communication and photonic quantum information processing, but many solid-state platforms still rely on bulky optical excitation, careful alignment, and post-selection to achieve useful linewidth, stability, and brightness. Scalable quantum photonics instead requires turnkey quantum-light engines that can be triggered on demand, stabilized against environmental noise, and efficiently interfaced with fibers or photonic circuits. This review surveys recent progress in electronic and photonic integration of single quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials, focusing on localized excitonic emitters in transition metal dichalcogenides and defect-based color centers in hexagonal boron nitride. On the electronic side, we discuss electrical injection, fast modulation, electrostatic stabilization, and Stark tunability as routes to suppress blinking, spectral wandering, and charge-noise-induced broadening. On the photonic side, we review waveguide and resonator platforms that funnel emission into well-defined optical modes and, in some cases, enhance radiative rates through the Purcell effect. We connect these integration strategies to key source metrics, including single-photon purity, brightness, spectral stability, and photon indistinguishability. We conclude that the next stage of progress will depend on co-designed electronic and photonic architectures that jointly optimize on-demand operation, stabilization, tunability, and packaging-compatible optical interfacing.

AI.tldr: This review surveys recent progress in electronic and photonic integration of single quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials, focusing on TMDs and hBN, and argues that future progress requires co-designed electronic-photonic architectures for turnkey quantum-light sources.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum photonics requires turnkey quantum-light engines that are on-demand, stable, and efficiently interfaced with fibers/photonic circuits, yet many solid-state platforms still rely on bulky optics, alignment, and post-selection.
AI.method: The review surveys electronic integration (electrical injection, modulation, electrostatic stabilization, Stark tunability) and photonic integration (waveguide/resonator platforms, Purcell enhancement) of single quantum emitters in 2D materials (TMDs and hBN).
AI.result: Key source metrics—single-photon purity, brightness, spectral stability, and photon indistinguishability—are connected to specific integration strategies.
AI.conclusion: The next stage of progress depends on co-designed electronic and photonic architectures that jointly optimize on-demand operation, stabilization, tunability, and packaging-compatible optical interfacing.

title: Weighted Phase-Space Paths for Exact Wigner Dynamics
summary: A quantum state can be written in phase space, but the resulting object is not generally the probability density of a positive stochastic process on ordinary phase space. We spell this out for Wigner dynamics. If a positive phase-space process is required only to reproduce the Born density after integrating over momentum, the requirement fixes only an integrated current; the local drift and diffusion remain underdetermined. If one instead requires all Weyl-ordered expectation values, the phase-space object is fixed to be the Wigner function. For non-quadratic potentials the Wigner--Moyal generator contains higher-order, signed momentum-transfer terms, so it is not the Fokker--Planck generator of a positive Brownian diffusion. The exact Wigner function must therefore be reconstructed, in a stochastic representation, as a weighted empirical measure \[ \FW(\z,t)=\E_{\Pp}[W_tδ(\z-\z_t)], \qquad \z=(q,p), \] rather than the unweighted density of sampled carrier trajectories. With classical Hamiltonian flow as the carrier, all nonclassical correction beyond classical transport sits in the Moyal residual and can be represented by signed weights or branching events. The same split defines a residual diagnostic that vanishes for quadratic Hamiltonians and measures what classical carrier transport misses in anharmonic dynamics. The formulation also gives a forward--reverse relation for signed Wigner path measures. The ratio of forward and reversed contributions separates into a positive magnitude factor and a sign factor. This sign records the parity of the Wigner interference contribution; it is not a thermodynamic entropy production.

AI.tldr: This paper clarifies that the Wigner function in phase space is not a probability density for a positive stochastic process, but must be reconstructed as a weighted empirical measure with signed weights or branching events. It introduces a residual diagnostic for nonclassical effects, and shows that the forward-reverse ratio separates into a positive magnitude factor and a sign factor recording Wigner interference parity, not thermodynamic entropy production.
AI.motivation: To resolve the misconception that quantum states can be represented as positive probability densities of a stochastic process on ordinary phase space, and to clarify the mathematical structure and interpretation of Wigner dynamics and its stochastic representation.
AI.method: The paper analyzes Wigner dynamics from the perspective of stochastic processes in phase space, deriving conditions for positive phase-space processes, decomposing the Wigner-Moyal generator into classical Hamiltonian flow and Moyal residuals, and formulating a forward-reverse relation for signed Wigner path measures.
AI.result: A positive phase-space process reproducing Born density is underdetermined. The exact Wigner function requires a weighted empirical measure with signed weights or branching events. The forward-reverse ratio factorizes into a positive magnitude factor and a sign factor linked to Wigner interference parity, not entropy production.
AI.conclusion: The Wigner function is not a genuine probability density for a positive stochastic process; its stochastic representation involves signed weights. The proposed split and residual diagnostic quantify nonclassical corrections beyond classical transport, and the sign factor in forward-reverse relations is a quantum interference effect, distinct from thermodynamic irreversibility.

title: Optical Pulling Force in Carbon Nanotubes: Manifestation of Nonlocal Conductivity
summary: We develop a new theory of an optical force exerted on a carbon nanotube (CNT) with a nonlocal conductivity. The optical force is expressed in terms of the surface current density and the axial electric field on the CNT surface. To determine these quantities, we employ an integral-equation-based approach in terms of the current density. The analysis is constructed for a finite-length cylindrical CNT by rigorously accounting for edge effects. In addition to numerical solutions of the integral equation, we obtain an approximate analytical expression for the optical force acting on the CNT, which shows good agreement with numerical simulations. We also demonstrate the existence of some frequency ranges in which the optical force becomes negative, corresponding to the optical pulling effect. Such a pulling behavior is shown to originate from the nonlocality of the conductivity and to vanish in the local limit. This work advances theoretical understanding of optomechanical interactions in finite-length low-dimensional conductors and clarifies the role of spatial dispersion in the emergence of optical pulling forces.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of optical force on a finite-length carbon nanotube with nonlocal conductivity, using an integral-equation approach that accounts for edge effects. It finds that nonlocality enables negative optical forces (pulling effect), which vanish in the local limit.
AI.motivation: To advance theoretical understanding of optomechanical interactions in finite-length low-dimensional conductors and clarify how spatial dispersion (nonlocal conductivity) contributes to optical pulling forces.
AI.method: The optical force is expressed via surface current density and axial electric field on the CNT surface. An integral-equation-based approach in terms of current density is employed, with rigorous treatment of edge effects for a finite-length cylindrical CNT. Both numerical solutions and an approximate analytical expression are derived.
AI.result: The approximate analytical expression for optical force agrees well with numerical simulations. Certain frequency ranges exhibit negative optical force (pulling effect), which originates from nonlocal conductivity and vanishes in the local limit.
AI.conclusion: Nonlocal conductivity is essential for generating optical pulling forces on carbon nanotubes, and edge effects in finite-length conductors must be rigorously accounted for in such analyses.

title: Pontus-Mpemba effect in cavity quantum electrodynamics
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in Physica A (special issue Mpemba Effect: An Anomalous Relaxation Phenomenon)
summary: The quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon in which a quantum system relaxes faster through a two-step evolution protocol than through a single, unquenched relaxation. This work proposes its realization in cavity quantum electrodynamics using the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss. The model captures the coherent interaction between a two-level atom and a single quantized mode of a lossy cavity, providing a minimal yet realistic setting to explore dissipative quantum dynamics. Restricting the analysis to the single-excitation sector, the dynamics feature damped vacuum Rabi oscillations for weak dissipation that transition to near-exponential atomic decay under strong dissipation. A sudden quench of the cavity decay rate generates distinct relaxation trajectories from the same initial atom-cavity state. The atomic excitation then displays a non-monotonic, accelerated decay, where a trajectory with a quenched dissipation relaxes faster than fixed-loss evolution. The effect originates from the interplay between coherent atom-photon exchange and cavity dissipation, establishing a clear and experimentally accessible realization of the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect in both optical and circuit QED platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes realizing the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect—faster relaxation via a two-step quenching protocol—in cavity QED using the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss, where a sudden quench of cavity decay rate leads to accelerated atomic decay compared to fixed-loss evolution.
AI.motivation: To propose an experimentally accessible realization of the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect (faster relaxation through two-step quenching than single-step relaxation) in cavity quantum electrodynamics using the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss.
AI.method: Uses the Jaynes-Cummings model with photon loss, restricted to the single-excitation sector, with a sudden quench of the cavity decay rate to generate distinct relaxation trajectories from the same initial atom-cavity state.
AI.result: The atomic excitation displays non-monotonic, accelerated decay under a quenched dissipation protocol, where a trajectory with quenched dissipation relaxes faster than fixed-loss evolution, due to the interplay between coherent atom-photon exchange and cavity dissipation.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a clear and experimentally accessible realization of the quantum Pontus-Mpemba effect in both optical and circuit QED platforms.

title: Three wave mixing vacuum squeezing generation in a SNAIL-based Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier with alternated flux polarity
summary: Recent demonstrations of squeezing generation using Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifiers (TWPAs) have opened the way for the application of broadband microwave squeezing in quantum sensing, quantum-enhanced detection, and continuous-variable quantum information. Here we demonstrate vacuum squeezing generation via residual three-wave mixing (3WM) in a Josephson TWPA based on superconducting nonlinear asymmetric inductive elements (SNAILs) with alternated magnetic flux polarity. By investigating competition between four-wave mixing (4WM) and 3WM nonlinearities, we prove that vacuum squeezing generation via residual 3WM is possible when a careful choice of the operating flux point is adopted. Our study provides valuable insights on the impact of competing nonlinearities on TWPA squeezers, potentially extending the range of applications in the framework of microwave photonics.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates vacuum squeezing generation using residual three-wave mixing in a SNAIL-based Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier with alternated flux polarity, achieved by carefully selecting the operating flux point to balance competing 4WM and 3WM nonlinearities.
AI.motivation: To enable broadband microwave squeezing for applications in quantum sensing, quantum-enhanced detection, and continuous-variable quantum information by exploiting residual 3WM in TWPAs.
AI.method: Using a SNAIL-based Josephson TWPA with alternated magnetic flux polarity to generate vacuum squeezing via residual three-wave mixing (3WM), while investigating the competition between 4WM and 3WM nonlinearities.
AI.result: Vacuum squeezing generation via residual 3WM is achievable when the operating flux point is carefully chosen to manage the competition between 4WM and 3WM.
AI.conclusion: The study provides insights into the impact of competing nonlinearities on TWPA squeezers, potentially expanding applications in microwave photonics.

title: Non-Abelian String-Breaking Dynamics on a Qudit Quantum Computer
summary: Gauge theories form the foundation of the Standard Model of particle physics. These theories can exhibit confinement, where charged particles only occur in bound states, connected by flux strings whose energy grows linearly with separation. Simulating the real-time dynamics of such strings, including their breaking, remains a major challenge for classical computations and a promising target for quantum simulations. While recent quantum simulation experiments explored string-breaking dynamics in abelian lattice gauge theories, non-abelian theories are qualitatively distinct because gauge fields themselves carry charge. Here, we report the first quantum simulation of genuine non-abelian string-breaking dynamics in a pure SU($2$) lattice gauge theory, where gauge-field self-interactions drive string breaking even in the absence of dynamical matter. Our results are obtained on a trapped-ion quantum computer, using native qudit Hilbert spaces to encode truncated gauge fields on a ladder geometry and implement digital Trotter dynamics. We experimentally study unbreakable and breakable strings generated by fundamental and adjoint static charges, respectively. We locally resolve string oscillations and coherent string breaking through the creation of gluonic excitations driven by non-abelian plaquette interactions. Our work establishes hardware-efficient, problem-tailored qudit simulations as a promising route for accessing non-perturbative dynamics relevant to high-energy physics.

AI.tldr: First quantum simulation of genuine non-abelian string-breaking dynamics in pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory using trapped-ion qudit quantum computer, demonstrating gauge-field self-interactions drive string breaking without dynamical matter.
AI.motivation: Real-time dynamics of flux strings and their breaking in non-abelian gauge theories is a major challenge for classical computation and a promising target for quantum simulation, yet previous quantum experiments have only explored abelian theories where gauge fields are neutral.
AI.method: Implemented digital Trotter dynamics on a trapped-ion quantum computer using native qudit Hilbert spaces to encode truncated gauge fields on a ladder geometry for pure SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
AI.result: Demonstrated unbreakable and breakable strings from fundamental and adjoint static charges respectively; locally resolved string oscillations and coherent string breaking via gluonic excitations driven by non-abelian plaquette interactions.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-efficient, problem-tailored qudit simulations offer a promising route for accessing non-perturbative high-energy physics dynamics.

title: Surface-Code Thresholds and Qubit Footprints in Shuttling-Based Spin-Qubit Railways
summary: We present a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a $2\times N$ silicon spin-qubit railway architecture, utilizing electron shuttling to resolve the wiring fan-out bottleneck. Employing circuit-level noise modeling, we evaluate threshold performances across various noise biases. We demonstrate that shuttling check qubits instead of data qubits fundamentally improves system thresholds. Crucially, under a noise model biased towards dephasing for spin-qubit shuttling, the non-CSS XZZX surface code outperforms standard CSS variants. By tailoring the topological code to this specific inherent bias, we show that the Megaquop footprint is achievable with a distance 7 code requiring a $p = 10^{-3}$ physical error rate, highlighting a pathway for substantial hardware reductions in early fault-tolerant quantum processors.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fault-tolerant mapping of rotated surface codes onto a 2×N silicon spin-qubit railway architecture using electron shuttling, showing that shuttling check qubits improves thresholds and that the XZZX surface code outperforms CSS variants under dephasing-biased noise, achieving Megaquop footprint with distance 7 at p=10⁻³ error rate.
AI.motivation: To resolve the wiring fan-out bottleneck in silicon spin-qubit quantum architectures by leveraging electron shuttling, and to find a fault-tolerant mapping that achieves practical Megaquop-scale computation with minimal hardware overhead.
AI.method: The authors map rotated surface codes onto a 2×N railway architecture with electron shuttling, evaluate via circuit-level noise modeling across various noise biases, compare shuttling check vs. data qubits, and analyze XZZX non-CSS code performance under dephasing-biased noise for shuttling.
AI.result: Shuttling check qubits instead of data qubits fundamentally improves system thresholds. Under dephasing-biased noise for spin-qubit shuttling, the non-CSS XZZX surface code outperforms standard CSS variants. A Megaquop footprint is achievable with distance 7 at p=10⁻³ physical error rate.
AI.conclusion: Tailoring topological codes to the inherent noise bias of the hardware (dephasing in shuttling) enables substantial hardware reductions, providing a clear pathway toward early fault-tolerant quantum processors with reduced resource requirements.

title: Quantum-enhanced Large Language Models on Quantum Hardware via Cayley Unitary Adapters
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed artificial intelligence, yet classical architectures impose a fundamental constraint: every trainable parameter demands classical memory that scales unfavourably with model size. Quantum computing offers a qualitatively different pathway, but practical demonstrations on real hardware have remained elusive for models of practical relevance. Here we show that Cayley-parameterised unitary adapters -- quantum circuit blocks inserted into the frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs and executed on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two superconducting processor -- improve the perplexity of Llama 3.1 8B, an 8-billion-parameter model in widespread use, by 1.4% with only 6,000 additional parameters and end-to-end inference validated on real Quantum Processing Unit (QPU). A systematic study on SmolLM2 (135M parameters), chosen for its tractability, reveals monotonically improving perplexity with unitary block dimension, 83% recovery of compression-induced degradation, and correct answers to questions that both classical baselines fail -- with a sharp noise-expressivity phase transition identifying the concrete path to quantum utility at larger qubit scales.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that Cayley-parameterized unitary adapters (quantum circuit blocks) inserted into frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs and executed on a 156-qubit IBM superconducting processor improve perplexity by 1.4% on Llama 3.1 8B using only 6,000 additional parameters, with end-to-end inference validated on real QPU. A systematic study on SmolLM2 reveals monotonic perplexity improvement with block dimension, 83% recovery of compression-induced degradation, and a noise-expressivity phase transition pointing toward quantum utility at larger scales.
AI.motivation: Classical LLMs require memory that scales unfavorably with parameter count. Quantum computing offers a different pathway, but practical demonstrations on real hardware for models of practical relevance have remained elusive.
AI.method: Cayley-parameterized unitary adapters — quantum circuit blocks inserted into frozen projection layers of pre-trained LLMs — executed on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum System Two superconducting processor.
AI.result: 1.4% perplexity improvement on Llama 3.1 8B with only 6,000 additional parameters; monotonic perplexity improvement with unitary block dimension on SmolLM2; 83% recovery of compression-induced degradation; correct answers to questions that classical baselines fail; identification of a noise-expressivity phase transition.
AI.conclusion: Quantum adapters can benefit large-scale practical LLMs on current noisy quantum hardware, with a concrete path to quantum utility at larger qubit scales identified via the noise-expressivity phase transition.

title: Architecture Shape Governs QNN Trainability: Jacobian Null Space Growth and Parameter Efficiency
summary: Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding implement truncated Fourier series, and architectures arranging $N$ qubits with $L$ encoding layers each -- sharing encoding budget $E = NL$ -- generate identical frequency spectra, identical frequency redundancy, and require the same minimum parameter count for coefficient control. Despite this equivalence, trainability varies substantially with architecture shape $(N,L)$ at fixed $E$. We identify structural rank deficiency of the coefficient matching Jacobian $J$ as the mechanism responsible. For serial single-qubit architectures, we prove $\mathrm{rank}(J) \leq 2L+1$ regardless of parameter count $P$, with $\dim(\ker J) \geq P-(2L+1)$ growing without bound -- a phenomenon we term \emph{structural gradient starvation}: a growing fraction of parameters become structurally decoupled from the loss as $P$ increases at fixed $L$. Parallel architectures avoid this via independent phase trajectories, ensuring $σ_{\min}(J^{(\mathrm{par})}) > 0$ generically for $P \leq 2E+1$, so no parameter lies in $\ker J$. For practitioners, we further show that the two natural routes to increasing parameter count have fundamentally different effects: adding feature map (FM) layers monotonically strengthens the Jacobian QFIM eigenvalue spectrum and achieves $R^2 \geq 0.95$ with $1.6$--$2.2\times$ fewer parameters than adding trainable blocks across all tested architectures, while trainable blocks improve training only through the classical interpolation mechanism with no quantum-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: Variational quantum circuits with angle encoding produce identical frequency spectra at fixed encoding budget $E=NL$, but trainability varies with architecture shape $(N,L)$. Serial architectures suffer from "structural gradient starvation" where $\mathrm{rank}(J) \leq 2L+1$ causes a growing fraction of parameters to decouple from the loss. Parallel architectures avoid this via independent phase trajectories. Adding feature map layers strengthens the Jacobian spectrum and uses 1.6–2.2× fewer parameters than adding trainable blocks, which provide only classical interpolation benefits.
AI.motivation: To understand why variational quantum circuit architectures with identical frequency spectra and encoding budgets exhibit substantially different trainability, and to identify the mechanism underlying this discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors analyze the structural rank deficiency of the coefficient matching Jacobian $J$, prove theoretical bounds for serial single-qubit architectures ($\mathrm{rank}(J) \leq 2L+1$), derive $\dim(\ker J) \geq P-(2L+1)$ for growing parameter counts, and compare parallel architectures which avoid this deficiency. They empirically contrast adding feature map (FM) layers versus trainable blocks.
AI.result: Serial architectures exhibit structural gradient starvation where increasing parameters at fixed $L$ causes a growing fraction to become decoupled from the loss. Parallel architectures ensure $\sigma_{\min}(J^{(\mathrm{par})}) > 0$ for $P \leq 2E+1$. FM layers strengthen the Jacobian QFIM spectrum and achieve $R^2 \geq 0.95$ with 1.6–2.2× fewer parameters than adding trainable blocks, which offer no quantum-specific benefit.
AI.conclusion: Architecture design choices at fixed encoding budget critically determine trainability through Jacobian rank properties. Adding feature map layers is a fundamentally more efficient way to improve performance than adding trainable blocks, as the latter only provides classical interpolation benefits.

title: Passive Imaging with Quantum Advantage
summary: Far-field optical imaging inevitably involves low-pass spatial filtering, limiting the resolution. Moreover, conventional imaging suppresses high spatial frequency components close to the cutoff, making them invisible under noise, particularly the shot noise arising from discrete and random nature of quantum light. Here we propose and implement a method for reducing the effect of this noise by optically pre-processing the incoming light prior to detection, thereby optimizing the quantum measurement performed on it. Our scheme, termed Fourier Domain Division (FDD), partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection and subsequent post-processing for image reconstruction. By analyzing the quantum and classical Fisher information, we show that our method is advantageous with respect to direct imaging for high spatial-frequency components. As a result, the number of photons required to achieve a certain signal-to-noise-ratio in the Fourier domain is reduced, thus enhancing the overall resolution in the photon-starved regime. We demonstrate our method in microscopy, achieving 5-fold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components. Unlike active super-resolution methods, FDD is passive, making it broadly applicable in microscopy and other imaging scenarios where active illumination is impractical, including astronomy and remote sensing. Our work establishes a general strategy for designing quantum optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits, practical image analysis and computer vision applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Fourier Domain Division (FDD), a passive optical preprocessing method that partitions the Fourier plane for independent detection, enhancing resolution in photon-starved imaging by improving Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components and reducing shot noise effects.
AI.motivation: Far-field optical imaging is limited by low-pass spatial filtering and shot noise from quantum light, which suppresses high spatial frequency components near the cutoff frequency, making them invisible under noise.
AI.method: FDD partitions the Fourier plane into multiple regions for independent detection, followed by post-processing for image reconstruction. The method analyzes quantum and classical Fisher information to optimize the quantum measurement.
AI.result: Achieved 5-fold improvement of Fisher information on high spatial-frequency components in microscopy; reduced photon count required for a given SNR in the Fourier domain, enhancing overall resolution in the photon-starved regime.
AI.conclusion: FDD establishes a general strategy for designing quantum-optimized superresolution imaging systems, bridging fundamental quantum limits with practical imaging applications, and is broadly applicable to microscopy, astronomy, and remote sensing.

title: Syndrome resampling enhances quantum error correction thresholds
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) enables fault-tolerant quantum computation but requires operating quantum hardware at physical error rates below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. We introduce syndrome resampling, a general method that increases QEC thresholds of any decoder and suppresses logical errors without additional hardware, decoding modifications, or code-specific assumptions beyond syndrome statistics. The method exploits the fact that syndromes with low probability are likely to lead to logical failure, therefore biasing syndrome averages towards most likely syndromes effectively increases logical fidelities. We establish a direct connection between the Rényi coherent information (RCI) and powers of the syndrome probability distribution, showing that resampling syndromes according to these powers combined with maximum likelihood decoding (MLD) realizes a family of optimal thresholds associated with phase transitions in the RCI. Numerical simulations of surface codes demonstrate that syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal decoders and reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in experimentally relevant regimes. We further show that syndrome resampling can be effectively implemented from finite data and combined with decoding-based post-selection to achieve additional gains. Finally, applying the method to existing experimental QEC data yields up to two orders of magnitude reduction in logical error rates without requiring additional measurements. Our results provide a practical and decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments.

AI.tldr: Syndrome resampling is introduced as a general method to increase QEC thresholds and suppress logical errors by biasing syndrome statistics toward most likely syndromes, without requiring additional hardware or decoding modifications.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction requires operating hardware below code-dependent thresholds, which remains challenging for current devices. The goal is to improve logical fidelities without additional hardware overhead or code-specific modifications.
AI.method: The method resamples syndromes according to powers of their probability distribution, leveraging the connection between Rényi coherent information and syndrome statistics. It biases averages toward high-probability syndromes and can be combined with any decoder, including maximum likelihood decoding and suboptimal decoders, as well as post-selection.
AI.result: Syndrome resampling substantially increases thresholds for both optimal and suboptimal surface code decoders, reduces logical error rates by up to four orders of magnitude in simulations, and achieves up to two orders of magnitude reduction on existing experimental QEC data.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome resampling provides a practical, decoder-agnostic route to improved logical fidelities in near-term QEC experiments without requiring additional hardware or measurements.

title: Variationally Compressing Quantum Circuits to Approximate Nonadiabatic Molecular Quantum Dynamics
summary: Quantum simulation has begun to penetrate the field of quantum chemistry in hopes of efficiently calculating ground state energies and approximating real-time evolution. With modern research highlighting nonadiabatic dynamics, tunably approximating deep circuits representing potential landscapes becomes crucial for simulating real quantum systems. Variationally approximating unitaries allows for shallower circuits and accuracy tunable to hardware fidelity, so long as the observable quantities are preserved. We show the variational compression of Trotter terms preserve reaction rate coefficients via classical emulation of a hybrid quantum-classical optimization method, as well as fast-forwarded adiabatic dynamics on quantum hardware. Compressed circuits can be incorporated with product-formula-based time evolution to approximate dynamics of a particle in two coupled harmonic potentials, allowing tunability when removing high-cost qubit interactions. Approximate rate coefficients are recovered after substituting terms in a nonadiabatic dynamic process, giving proof-of-principle for observable preservation under variational optimization. Attention is paid to minimizing qubit and gate-count resources.

AI.tldr: Variational compression of Trotter terms preserves reaction rate coefficients in nonadiabatic quantum dynamics, demonstrated via classical emulation and quantum hardware experiments, enabling tunable, resource-efficient quantum simulations.
AI.motivation: Nonadiabatic dynamics require deep quantum circuits to represent potential landscapes, but hardware fidelity limits circuit depth. Efficiently approximating these circuits while preserving observable quantities is crucial for practical quantum simulation of real chemical systems.
AI.method: The authors use variational compression of Trotter terms within a hybrid quantum-classical optimization framework. Compressed circuits are integrated with product-formula-based time evolution to simulate a particle in two coupled harmonic potentials. Both classical emulation and fast-forwarded adiabatic dynamics on quantum hardware are employed.
AI.result: Approximate reaction rate coefficients are recovered after substituting compressed terms in nonadiabatic dynamics, demonstrating observable preservation under variational optimization. The method enables tunable accuracy while minimizing qubit and gate-count resources.
AI.conclusion: Variational compression of unitary operators is a viable strategy for preserving chemically relevant observables (e.g., rate coefficients) while reducing circuit depth, providing a proof-of-principle for resource-efficient quantum simulation of nonadiabatic dynamics.

title: Matrix encoding method in variational algorithm of calculating eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues
summary:
We propose a variational method for constructing the eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues for an arbitrary $N\times N$ complex matrix. The quantum part of our algorithm is based on encoding the matrix elements into the pure state of a quantum system and expressing the loss function with optimization parameters in terms of certain probability amplitudes in the superposition state. The principal step of this algorithm is the measurement of the ancilla state
  that removes all extra terms from the above superposition and allows to probabilistically construct the required loss function along with its derivatives with respect to the optimization parameters. These output data are used to find the new values of optimization parameters for the next iteration of the loss function in the gradient optimization method. The depth and size of the circuit for this algorithm are, respectively, $O(N^2 \log N)$ and $O(\log N)$.

AI.tldr: A variational quantum algorithm for computing eigenvalues and generalized eigenvalues of arbitrary N×N complex matrices, using a loss function derived from probability amplitudes and ancilla measurement, with O(N² log N) depth and O(log N) circuit size.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum method capable of handling arbitrary complex matrices (not limited to Hermitian) for eigenvalue problems, leveraging variational principles to reduce quantum resource requirements.
AI.method: Matrix elements are encoded into pure quantum states. A loss function is expressed via probability amplitudes in a superposition state. Ancilla measurement removes extra terms, enabling probabilistic construction of the loss function and its gradients for gradient-based optimization.
AI.result: Circuit depth scales as O(N² log N) and circuit size as O(log N) for an N×N matrix.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational quantum algorithm provides a resource-efficient approach to eigenvalue and generalized eigenvalue problems for arbitrary complex matrices, suitable for near-term quantum devices.

title: Universal Analog Quantum Simulation
summary: Analog quantum simulators emulate complex many-body dynamics through native continuous-time evolution under hardware-defined interactions. Yet once a platform is specified, its interaction structure is largely fixed by the underlying hardware, restricting the Hamiltonians that can be realized and limiting programmability. Here we introduce universal analog quantum simulation (UAQS), a hybrid framework that systematically expands the range of accessible quantum evolutions within a given analog platform. UAQS employs optimized continuous-time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly, avoiding decomposition into discrete gate sequences. By preserving native analog evolution while extending the set of achievable Hamiltonians, UAQS transforms fixed-interaction analog devices into programmable simulators. Numerical studies on representative architectures, including superconducting circuits and Rydberg-atom arrays, show that UAQS accurately reproduces non-trivial many-body dynamics beyond the intrinsic interaction structure of the hardware. These results establish UAQS as a practical route toward programmable analog quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: UAQS is a hybrid framework that uses optimized continuous-time control fields to expand the Hamiltonian programmability of fixed-interaction analog quantum simulators, enabling simulation of dynamics beyond native hardware interactions.
AI.motivation: Analog quantum simulators are limited by fixed hardware-defined interaction structures, restricting the range of Hamiltonians that can be realized and thus limiting programmability.
AI.method: UAQS employs optimized continuous-time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly, preserving native analog evolution while extending achievable Hamiltonians without discrete gate decomposition.
AI.result: Numerical studies on superconducting circuits and Rydberg-atom arrays show UAQS accurately reproduces non-trivial many-body dynamics beyond the intrinsic interaction structure of the hardware.
AI.conclusion: UAQS establishes a practical route toward programmable analog quantum simulation by transforming fixed-interaction analog devices into programmable simulators.

title: Finite-size general security for differential phase shift keying via variable-length quantum key distribution
summary: Differential phase shift keying (DPSK) constitutes a pathway towards practical quantum key distribution by using affordable commercial technologies, and robust theoretical foundations. Recent advances in the security of DPSK have proven its security against general adversaries, albeit requiring limitations, including strong repetition rate constraints at the security proof and costly statistical estimators. In this work, we overcome said limitations by leveraging recent techniques in variable-length general security by using entropy accumulation techniques based on Rényi leftover hashing, together with conic optimization methods. Our approach achieves secret key rates with $10^5$ signals beyond 12 dB, constituting a robust proof of the experimental implementability of industrial-grade DPSK.

AI.tldr: This paper enhances DPSK-based quantum key distribution by combining variable-length general security analysis, entropy accumulation via Rényi leftover hashing, and conic optimization, achieving secret key rates with 10^5 signals beyond 12 dB and proving industrial-grade implementability.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of prior DPSK security proofs, specifically strong repetition rate constraints and costly statistical estimators, which hindered practical deployment.
AI.method: Leverages variable-length general security analysis, entropy accumulation techniques based on Rényi leftover hashing, and conic optimization methods.
AI.result: Achieves secret key rates with 10^5 signals beyond 12 dB.
AI.conclusion: Provides a robust proof of the experimental implementability of industrial-grade DPSK quantum key distribution.

title: Meromorphic Quantum Computing
summary: We consider the kinematic axioms of quantum mechanics projectively. Instead of normalized (pure) states up to global phase, states become one-dimensional subspaces of vector spaces. This process of projectivization is functorial and lax monoidal. For qubits it identifies the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere. We interpret a fragment of the ZXW-calculus projectively and thereby provide an alternate derivation of the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus of Coecke et al. We find meromorphic functions that characterize the coherent behaviour of circuits for logical state preparation of quantum codes and magic state distillation.

AI.tldr: The paper projectivizes quantum mechanical kinematic axioms, making state spaces one-dimensional subspaces rather than normalized states. This process is functorial and lax monoidal, identifying the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere for qubits. The authors interpret a fragment of the ZXW-calculus projectively, deriving the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus, and find meromorphic functions characterizing coherent behavior in logical state preparation and magic state distillation circuits.
AI.motivation: To reinterpret quantum mechanical kinematic axioms projectively, moving from normalized pure states (up to global phase) to one-dimensional subspaces, thereby establishing a cleaner mathematical foundation that connects projective geometry to quantum computing formalisms like the ZXW-calculus.
AI.method: The authors employ functorial and lax monoidal projectivization of quantum state spaces. For qubits, this identifies the Bloch sphere with the Riemann sphere. A fragment of the ZXW-calculus is interpreted projectively to derive the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus. Meromorphic functions are used to characterize coherent behavior in circuits for logical state preparation and magic state distillation.
AI.result: They derive the arithmetic GHZ/W-calculus from a projective interpretation of the ZXW-calculus. They identify meromorphic functions that describe the coherent behavior of circuits used for logical state preparation of quantum codes and magic state distillation.
AI.conclusion: Projectivization of quantum kinematics provides a unifying mathematical perspective linking projective geometry, the ZXW-calculus, and practical quantum protocols such as state preparation and magic state distillation, with meromorphic functions naturally describing circuit behavior.

title: Beating noise in frequency estimation with squeezing and memory in continuous-variable systems
summary: Quantum metrology promises precision beyond classical limits, yet environmental noise typically degrades the quantum resources required for such enhancement. In this work, we investigate frequency estimation in noisy continuous-variable systems, focusing on two complementary strategies to mitigate decoherence: Hamiltonian engineering and the exploitation of non-Markovian dynamics. By embedding squeezing directly into the system Hamiltonian, we show that the quantum Fisher information (QFI) may acquire a tunable higher-order time dependence, leading to enhanced sensitivity in the short-time regime. Moving beyond the Markovian approximation, we employ the quantum Brownian motion model to demonstrate that structured environments with finite memory can induce information backflow, temporarily restoring and even improving estimation precision relative to the unitary limit. We further assess the achievability of these bounds via Gaussian measurements, identifying regimes where homodyne, heterodyne, and optimized general-dyne measurements saturate the QFI, and noting that stronger squeezing widens the gap, potentially requiring non-Gaussian measurement strategies. Our results establish that jointly tailoring system Hamiltonian and environmental memory offers a viable route toward robust quantum-enhanced frequency estimation in open systems.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that combining Hamiltonian engineering (embedding squeezing into the system Hamiltonian) and leveraging non-Markovian dynamics (quantum Brownian motion model with finite memory) can enhance frequency estimation precision in noisy continuous-variable systems, achieving sensitivity beyond the unitary limit in certain regimes. The achievability of these bounds via Gaussian measurements is analyzed, with stronger squeezing potentially requiring non-Gaussian strategies.
AI.motivation: Quantum metrology promises precision beyond classical limits, but environmental noise degrades the required quantum resources. The authors aim to mitigate decoherence in frequency estimation for noisy continuous-variable systems by jointly tailoring Hamiltonian engineering and exploiting non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.method: The authors investigate two complementary strategies: (1) Hamiltonian engineering by embedding squeezing directly into the system Hamiltonian, and (2) exploiting non-Markovian dynamics using the quantum Brownian motion model with finite memory. They analyze the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and assess achievability via Gaussian measurements (homodyne, heterodyne, optimized general-dyne).
AI.result: Hamiltonian engineering yields a tunable higher-order time dependence in QFI, enhancing short-time sensitivity. Non-Markovian dynamics induce information backflow that can temporarily restore and even improve estimation precision beyond the unitary limit. Stronger squeezing widens the gap between Gaussian-achievable precision and the QFI bound, potentially requiring non-Gaussian measurements.
AI.conclusion: Jointly tailoring the system Hamiltonian and environmental memory provides a viable route toward robust quantum-enhanced frequency estimation in open systems.

title: Local distillation from Reed Muller codes unfolding
summary: We generalize the unfolding of a Reed Muller distillation factory of Ruiz et. al. by exhibiting the algebraic structure that the unfolding is based on. We describe a 2D local layout for the Z stabilizers of a distance 4 Reed Muller distillation factory and a 3D local layout for the Z stabilizer of a distance 4 and a distance 7 Reed Muller distillation factory. Given input T states with infidelities $p=10^{-3}$, the 2D local distillation factory with distance 4 outputs a CCZ state with infidelity $p=8.256 \times 10^{-9}$ and the 3D local distillation factory with distance 7 outputs a T state with infidelity $p=1.1811 \times 10^{-17}$.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes the unfolding of Reed-Muller distillation factories by revealing the underlying algebraic structure, and presents 2D and 3D local layouts for Z stabilizers of various distances, achieving high-fidelity CCZ and T state outputs from noisy T state inputs.
AI.motivation: To generalize and improve upon the existing Reed-Muller distillation factory design by Ruiz et al. through exposing its algebraic foundation and enabling more efficient physical layouts for magic state distillation.
AI.method: The authors generalize the unfolding process by identifying the algebraic structure it is based on, then construct a 2D local layout for Z stabilizers of a distance-4 factory and a 3D local layout for Z stabilizers of distance-4 and distance-7 factories.
AI.result: With input T states at infidelity p=10^{-3}, the 2D distance-4 factory produces a CCZ state at infidelity 8.256×10^{-9}, and the 3D distance-7 factory produces a T state at infidelity 1.1811×10^{-17}.
AI.conclusion: The algebraic structure enables systematic unfolding of Reed-Muller distillation factories, and the local layouts demonstrate substantial fidelity improvements for both CCZ and T state distillation across different distances and dimensions.

title: Macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes via two-tone driving of a superconducting qubit
summary: The cavity-mediated coupling between magnons in an yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) sphere and a superconducting qubit has recently been demonstrated as a new platform for preparing macroscopic quantum states. Here, based on this system, we propose to entangle two magnon modes in two YIG spheres by driving the qubit with a two-tone field and by appropriately choosing the frequencies and strengths of the two driving fields. We show that strong entanglement can be achieved with fully feasible parameters. We further provide a detection scheme for experimentally verifying the entanglement. Our results indicate that macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes in two millimeter-sized YIG spheres, involving more than $10^{18}$ spins, can be realized using currently available parameters, which finds promising applications in fundamental studies, such as macroscopic quantum mechanics and the test of unconventional decoherence theories.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to entangle two magnon modes in two YIG spheres using a superconducting qubit driven by a two-tone field, achieving strong entanglement with feasible parameters and providing a detection scheme. This involves over 10^18 spins, enabling macroscopic quantum state preparation.
AI.motivation: To prepare and verify macroscopic quantum states by entangling two magnon modes in millimeter-sized YIG spheres, enabling fundamental studies in macroscopic quantum mechanics and tests of unconventional decoherence theories.
AI.method: Using cavity-mediated coupling between magnons in YIG spheres and a superconducting qubit, driving the qubit with a two-tone field with appropriately chosen frequencies and strengths to entangle two magnon modes.
AI.result: Strong entanglement between two magnon modes can be achieved with fully feasible parameters, involving over 10^18 spins in two millimeter-sized YIG spheres.
AI.conclusion: Macroscopic entanglement between two magnon modes in two YIG spheres is realizable with currently available parameters, offering promising applications in macroscopic quantum mechanics and tests of unconventional decoherence theories.

title: Ablation Removal of Transport-Blocking Defects in Surface-Electrode Ion Traps
summary: We demonstrate in situ removal of a transport-blocking defect on a surface-electrode ion trap device using a Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser. This approach eliminates the need to vent and rebake the vacuum system, providing a low-overhead defect-remediation technique well suited for ion-shuttling architectures where system modifications typically incur substantial downtime - particularly in shuttling focussed experiments operating at temperatures that necessitate bakes. Additionally, the hardware used is readily available in many ion trap laboratories, making this solution attractive to experiments operating in such regimes. Following ablation, we observe near-unit shuttling success rates across the previously obstructed region and measure micromotion levels that remain within acceptable limits. This technique enables rapid, reliable restoration of transport pathways without interruption to experimental operation.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates using a Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser to remove transport-blocking defects on surface-electrode ion traps in situ, eliminating the need for venting and rebaking, with near-unit shuttling success and acceptable micromotion levels.
AI.motivation: To develop a low-overhead defect-remediation technique that avoids the costly downtime of venting and rebaking vacuum systems in ion-shuttling architectures, particularly for experiments operating at temperatures requiring bakes.
AI.method: A Q-switched Nd:YAG 532 nm pulsed ablation laser is used to ablate transport-blocking defects directly on a surface-electrode ion trap in situ, without breaking vacuum.
AI.result: Near-unit shuttling success rates were achieved across the previously obstructed region, and micromotion levels remained within acceptable limits after ablation.
AI.conclusion: This technique enables rapid, reliable restoration of transport pathways without experimental interruption, using hardware already common in ion trap laboratories.

title: Coherence limitations of a Fourier-engineered $\cos(2\varphi)$ transmon qubit
summary: Intrinsically protected superconducting qubits are a promising route toward enhancing coherence times and advancing hardware towards applications in quantum computing. The $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit achieves protection against qubit relaxation by allowing only the coherent tunneling of pairs of Cooper pairs, resulting in Cooper-pair parity symmetry and thereby suppressing charge-induced errors. In this work, we experimentally realize a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit by Fourier engineering the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction superconducting circuit. Using an interference-based architecture, we are able to suppress the odd harmonics of an effective qubit potential and we observe good agreement between the measured transition spectrum and the effective theoretical model. We further investigate the energy relaxation time as a function of external flux and find that the qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point is limited by $1/f$ flux noise. This strong sensitivity arises from residual fluctuations in the first harmonic, which possesses a large prefactor despite being nominally canceled. In contrast, a fluxonium qubit with a similar energy spectrum and noise amplitude is less affected by flux noise, highlighting a key challenge for interference-based protection schemes.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally realizes a $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit using Fourier engineering in a multi-junction superconducting circuit. The qubit suppresses odd harmonics for protection against charge-induced errors via Cooper-pair parity symmetry. However, despite nominally canceling the first harmonic, residual fluctuations cause strong sensitivity to $1/f$ flux noise, limiting qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point. Compared to a fluxonium qubit with similar spectrum, this scheme shows greater vulnerability to flux noise, highlighting a key challenge for interference-based protection.
AI.motivation: To enhance coherence times in quantum computing by realizing intrinsically protected superconducting qubits that suppress charge-induced errors through Cooper-pair parity symmetry, leveraging the $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubit approach.
AI.method: Fourier engineering of the energy-phase relation in a multi-junction superconducting circuit using an interference-based architecture to suppress odd harmonics of the effective qubit potential.
AI.result: The qubit lifetime at the flux symmetry point is limited by $1/f$ flux noise due to residual fluctuations in the first harmonic, which has a large prefactor despite nominal cancellation.
AI.conclusion: Interference-based protection schemes face a key challenge: residual first-harmonic fluctuations make $\cos(2\varphi)$ qubits more sensitive to flux noise than fluxonium qubits with similar energy spectra, indicating that alternative approaches may be needed for robust protection.

title: Photonic-Implemented Efficient Deep Quantum Neural Network via Virtual-Driven Hilbert Space Expansion
summary: The growing computational demands of classical neural networks have intensified the search for energy-efficient and powerful computational alternatives. Quantum neural networks (QNNs) implemented on integrated photonic platforms offer a compelling avenue, offering exceptional computational power enhancements, with inherent programmability and scalability of integrated architectures. A critical challenge, however, is implementing the fundamental non-unitary and nonlinear activation function of QNNs within a linear quantum photonic system. Existing strategies, such as the adding ancillary qubits and measurement-based feedback or forward are constrained by high qubit resource costs, overhead devices, and poor cascadability. Here, we propose a novel deep photonic QNN with an expanded computational Hilbert space via input replication and mode expansion, which enables the realization of effective non-unitary and nonlinear activation on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip. This approach eliminates the need for physical ancillary qubits, measurement-induced qubit consumption and the measurement device burden, thereby significantly reduce resource costs. The fabricated chip integrates four high-quality entanglement sources and a programmable high-dimensional interferometric network, enabling a two-hidden-layer QNN that exhibits dimension-enhanced expressivity over the existing QNN architectures. We demonstrate its capabilities across diverse tasks, including nonlinear classification, image generation, and quantum Gibbs state preparation. This work establishes a scalable and efficient architecture toward practical quantum deep learning systems capable of tackling problems beyond the reach of classical computation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deep photonic quantum neural network that uses input replication and mode expansion to realize non-unitary and nonlinear activation functions on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip, eliminating the need for ancillary qubits and measurement-based feedback, and demonstrates its capabilities in nonlinear classification, image generation, and quantum Gibbs state preparation.
AI.motivation: The growing computational demands of classical neural networks have driven the search for energy-efficient alternatives. While QNNs on integrated photonic platforms offer promise, implementing non-unitary and nonlinear activation functions in linear quantum photonic systems remains a critical challenge. Existing strategies using ancillary qubits and measurement-based feedback are limited by high qubit resource costs, overhead devices, and poor cascadability.
AI.method: The authors propose a deep photonic QNN that expands the computational Hilbert space via input replication and mode expansion, enabling effective non-unitary and nonlinear activation on a linear programmable quantum photonic chip without physical ancillary qubits or measurement-induced qubit consumption. The fabricated chip integrates four high-quality entanglement sources and a programmable high-dimensional interferometric network, implementing a two-hidden-layer QNN with dimension-enhanced expressivity.
AI.result: The chip demonstrates dimension-enhanced expressivity over existing QNN architectures and shows capabilities across diverse tasks including nonlinear classification, image generation, and quantum Gibbs state preparation.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a scalable and efficient architecture toward practical quantum deep learning systems capable of tackling problems beyond the reach of classical computation.

title: A Residual-Based Quantum Linear System Algorithm with Dynamic Stopping and Applications to Elliptic PDEs
summary:
Quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs) have rigorous worst-case complexity guarantees, but their runtimes are often chosen from spectral information assumed in advance. What is largely lacking is an a posteriori progress flag: most QLSA workflows, unlike the classical counterparts, do not provide a built-in mechanism to signal whether a particular instance has already converged.

title: Multitime memory beyond the quantum regression theorem in sequential measurement statistics
summary: We investigate the presence of memory in the sequential measurement statistics of an open quantum system, as witnessed by the departure from the quantum regression theorem (QRT), that is, the possibility to predict multitime probabilities from the one-time reduced dynamical map. For factorized initial states, we identify an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like contribution, fully determined by the reduced dynamical map, and a memory term encoding system--environment correlations across the intervention; in the weak-coupling regime, the memory term yields an explicit second-order correction expressed in terms of the reduced map and bath correlation functions. Furthermore, we introduce an operational quantifier of QRT violations based on the distance between exact and QRT-predicted joint probabilities. Benchmarking the framework on a spin--boson model and using a pseudomode embedding as nonperturbative reference, we comprehensively analyze the impact of spectral-density parameters, environmental temperature, and measurement protocols on the non-Markovianity of the multitime statistics. Comparison with a one-time quantifier shows that reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are related but inequivalent: the latter, as probed through sequential statistics, is intrinsically protocol dependent and can become visible at higher temporal order even when two-time statistics remain compatible with QRT predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory effects in open quantum systems beyond the quantum regression theorem (QRT), deriving an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like part and a memory term, computing a second-order weak-coupling correction, and introducing an operational quantifier for QRT violations. Using a spin-boson model with pseudomode embedding, they show that multitime memory is protocol-dependent and can appear at higher temporal orders even when two-time statistics satisfy QRT, demonstrating inequivalence with reduced-state non-Markovianity.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify memory in sequential measurement statistics of open quantum systems beyond the quantum regression theorem, and to characterize the relationship between multitime memory and standard reduced-state non-Markovianity.
AI.method: Exact decomposition of the two-time propagator; second-order weak-coupling perturbation theory; operational distance-based quantifier for QRT violations; numerical benchmarking on a spin-boson model with pseudomode embedding.
AI.result: Memory effects in multitime statistics are intrinsically protocol dependent; they can become visible at higher temporal orders even when two-time statistics remain compatible with QRT predictions; reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are related but inequivalent.
AI.conclusion: The QRT fails to capture multitime memory arising from system-environment correlations across interventions; a proper characterization of non-Markovianity requires analyzing sequential measurement statistics, not just the reduced dynamical map.

title: Revisiting the multi-mode rhombus circuit as a biased-noise qubit
summary: In this work, we revisit the idea of using an interferometer of pairs of Josephson junctions as a protected rhombus qubit. Unlike in the original proposal, where the qubit states are encoded into odd and even parity charge states, here, we intentionally alter the energy of one of the junctions to investigate the soft version of the rhombus qubit. This approach allows us to directly probe the qubit transitions over several GHz and reduce the potential drawbacks of the interferometer-based protection. Away from a half flux quantum external field, the large shunting capacitors of the circuit ensure localized qubit states in different phase valleys, leading to a biased-noise qubit. In the realized circuit, we measure an average $T_1\approx500\,μ$s relaxation time in the biased-noise regime (with a Ramsey dephasing time of $T^{R}_\varphi\approx90\,$ns), while an average $T_1\approx27\,μ$s relaxation time at frustration (with $T^{R}_\varphi\approx670\,$ns). Our loss analysis on this multi-mode circuit indicates that at low frequencies, flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling limit the relaxation times, pointing toward the presence of an optimal operating regime of around a few GHz.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the protected rhombus qubit using a Josephson junction interferometer, introducing a "soft" version by detuning one junction to enable direct qubit probing and reduce protection drawbacks. It demonstrates two distinct operating regimes: a biased-noise regime (T₁≈500μs, dephasing 90ns) and a frustrated regime (T₁≈27μs, dephasing 670ns), with loss analysis identifying flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling as limiting factors at low frequencies.
AI.motivation: To revisit and improve the original rhombus qubit design, which encodes qubit states in odd/even parity charge states, by intentionally altering one junction's energy to create a "soft" rhombus qubit that allows direct probing of qubit transitions over several GHz while mitigating interferometer-based protection drawbacks.
AI.method: The authors implement a Josephson junction pair interferometer with asymmetric junction energies, using large shunting capacitors to ensure localized qubit states in different phase valleys away from half-flux quantum external field, creating a biased-noise qubit. They characterize the circuit by measuring relaxation (T₁) and Ramsey dephasing (T_φ^R) times in both biased-noise and frustrated regimes.
AI.result: In the biased-noise regime: average T₁≈500μs, Ramsey dephasing T_φ^R≈90ns. At frustration (half-flux): average T₁≈27μs, Ramsey dephasing T_φ^R≈670ns. Loss analysis reveals flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling limit relaxation at low frequencies, suggesting optimal operation around a few GHz.
AI.conclusion: The soft rhombus qubit enables a trade-off between relaxation and dephasing times depending on operating regime, with an optimal operating point around a few GHz where the limitations from flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling are minimized.

title: Tight Contraction Rates for Primitive Channels under Quantum $f$-Divergences
summary: Data-processing inequalities capture the phenomenon that two probability distributions can only become less distinguishable under any common post-processing. For more fine-grained inequalities, one turns to strong data-processing inequality (SDPI) constants, which give the strongest inequalities for a given channel and reference state for a fixed measure of distinguishability. These quantities have been used to quantify the rate at which time-homogeneous Markov chains contract towards a fixed point both in the classical and quantum setting. In this work, we establish that quantum $f$-divergences satisfy a local reverse Pinsker inequality, which implies the asymptotic contraction rate of a primitive channel to its stationary state is upper bounded by the SDPI constant of any non-commutative $χ^2$-divergence. Using quantum-detailed balance, we establish a sufficient condition for these bounds to be tight. Finally, we apply these results to Petz, Matsumoto, and Hirche-Tomamichel $f$-divergences, establishing new and strengthening previously known results.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that quantum $f$-divergences satisfy a local reverse Pinsker inequality, linking asymptotic contraction rates of primitive quantum channels to SDPI constants of non-commutative $\chi^2$-divergences, with tightness conditions via quantum-detailed balance and applications to several $f$-divergences.
